video_title: Why It May Take a Crisis to Change the System feat. Cem Karsan | Systematic Investor | Ep.425
gist: Recorded two days after a Democratic midterm landslide with VIX up 25%, Cem Karsan argues the US faces four interlocking pressures (unsustainable debt, too-big-to-fail markets, populism, China) born of 40 years of supply-side economics, and that the administration's endgame is to lean on dollar dominance to 'print money, buy stocks' via state industrial policy. Because QE-scale policy has never been deployed without a crisis, he expects a meaningful crisis to be allowed to happen before June 2027, and says investors must abandon passive investing for resilient, diversified, hedged portfolios.

insights.claim: Markets were falling on the second day after the midterm elections, with the VIX up about 25% on the day, following a prior-day rally that the host suspected was driven only by people taking off hedges.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Hedge-removal rallies after events are fragile; the post-election relief bid reversed within a day.
insights.quote: VIX up 25% on the day, I know exactly what's causing that.

insights.claim: In early November (as of the 3rd), trend followers had a difficult start: the BTOP 50 was down 1.59% MTD (up 11.62% YTD), the CTA index down 1.81% (up 11.81% YTD), the trend index down 1.75% (up 12.39% YTD), and short-term traders down 77bp (up 4.39% YTD), hurt by oil reversals, a flight to safety into bonds, grains and currencies.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: CTAs remain solidly positive for 2026 despite November reversal losses in oil and bond-driven whipsaws.

insights.claim: As of the night before recording, the S&P 500 total return was up 1.44% for November and 13.37% YTD, MSCI World up 1.23% and about 12.25% YTD, and world government bonds up 39bp for November but down about 1% YTD.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Equities entered the post-midterm shock with strong YTD gains, leaving room for drawdown.

insights.claim: 2026 had been a vol-compressing year that was poor for volatility managers except those trading dispersion, but dispersion has become so expensive that many dispersion managers have stepped away from it.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Crowded, richly priced dispersion trades are a source of latent fragility as managers exit.
insights.quote: the problem with the dispersion strategies are that the price of dispersion has gotten so high

insights.claim: Karsan links multi-strat and long/short equity stress in October to index-level vol compression: as long/short equity has grown in size, index vol pressure pushes single stocks apart (high dispersion), straining liquidity and creating a major headwind for both long/short equity and index vol strategies.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Multi-strat drawdowns are structural to the vol regime, not idiosyncratic, and can unwind together.
insights.quote: We've now seen a tremendous amount of stress that's being exacerbated in long short equity as it grows to a size where the liquidity particularly given the pressures of vol at the index level is pushing you know everything away from each other.

insights.claim: The two days after the midterms were very flows-driven and extremely good for vol managers, and two such days in vol can make up for six months of bad performance, giving long-vol strategies a 'meh until great' payoff profile.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Long-vol carry pain is the price of convex payoffs that arrive in short bursts around regime breaks.
insights.quote: two days in vol space by the way can make up for uh six months of bad performance

insights.claim: Karsan sees the Democratic 'blue wave' as a potential release valve that lets building macro stress accelerate, and says the beginnings of that were visible in markets on the recording day.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: The election outcome is treated as a catalyst for macro stress, not a stabilizer.
insights.quote: Obviously the macro developments with this blue wave that happened uh opens the window and can be a release valve for a lot of the macro stress we've been seeing to accelerate

insights.claim: Karsan was surprised by the size of the Democratic midterm sweep: Republican turnout was very high, but many angry MAGA voters voted Democrat, confusing observers including the administration; he says the Lula populist wave should have been a warning sign.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Populist anger is crossing party lines, so high turnout no longer maps to partisan outcomes.
insights.quote: But what we saw was a ton of Republican angry MAGA voters coming and voting Democrat.

insights.claim: Karsan argues the White House's muted response reflects the margin: in a 52-48 or 50-50 Senate scenario the administration would have pulled every lever to contest, but a landslide leaves no meaningful way to contest.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Tail risk of a contested-election constitutional crisis receded because the result was lopsided.
insights.quote: There is no way to contest this election um in a meaningful way.

insights.claim: Karsan reads Trump's pre-election warning to 'expect a problem' if midterms go badly as a setup to blame Democrats, opening the window for the administration to step away from market support earlier and allow more market stress.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: The policy 'put' under markets may be deliberately withdrawn with Democrats as the political scapegoat.
insights.quote: And it opens the window for an earlier move, right? Uh for markets to have more stress and for them at least to step away.

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Bessent has been unusually silent for about two weeks around the midterms, while Trump has spoken negatively about markets for the first time since around February, which Karsan flags as a signal to listen closely to.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Absence of the usual verbal market support from Treasury is a tell that intervention may pause.
insights.quote: when's the last time Bessent didn't say anything for two weeks?

insights.claim: Karsan states the administration has been actively managing and manipulating markets, visible in its own P&L, and that the market has become dependent on that support and has reached the end of the line without more extreme measures.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Market resilience is policy-dependent; continuation requires escalated intervention.
insights.quote: And the market has become incredibly dependent on that support

themes.theme: Four pressures from 40 years of supply-side

insights.claim: Karsan identifies four interacting pressures on the US, all products of 40 years of supply-side economics: an accelerating unsustainable national debt with rising rates, a financialized economy where markets are too big to fail, populism forcing fiscal spending, and China challenging US dominance.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Policy responses to one pressure worsen the others, so piecemeal fixes fail.
insights.quote: They all largely come from the same thing, which is 40 years of supply side economics, right?

insights.claim: With roughly $300 trillion of combined public and private equity, a 20% market rise adds about $50 trillion of liquidity and a 20% fall removes about $50 trillion, making markets more relevant than the real economy and too big to fail.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Wealth effects now dominate the economy, so policymakers cannot tolerate deep drawdowns.
insights.quote: We now have a $300 trillion equity private and public market.

insights.claim: Karsan argues earnings and growth have become narrow and fragile because they are tied to capex that is itself tied to the valuation gains of the names receiving equity inflows.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: A reflexive loop between valuations and capex means a valuation shock hits real earnings too.
insights.quote: that's why earnings uh and growth and everything has become so narrow and fragile

insights.claim: Populism makes the debt problem harder to resolve and pushes toward taxing the rich to give to the poor, which is a direct danger to equities in a market that is too big to fail.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Redistribution pressure is a structural headwind for profit margins and equity multiples.

insights.claim: Karsan's generational framework: as the pendulum swings to an extreme, the generation that grows into political dominance prioritizes median over mean outcomes, producing protectionism, then global conflict, then commodity crises; he says millennial political dominance peaks in roughly nine to ten years.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Populist pressure is a decade-long tailwind, not a one-cycle event.
insights.quote: you get more and more pressure to prioritize median outcomes instead of mean outcomes.

insights.claim: Karsan frames the root cause as human nature, not left-right politics: an irreconcilable conflict between nature (progress, survival of the fittest) and fairness, which makes the pendulum overshoot in both directions and ultimately break things when it swings back.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Expect overshoot: the swing back toward redistribution will go too far, as the supply-side swing did.
insights.quote: So it's not it's not left right, it's not politics, it's not it it it's way bigger than that.

insights.claim: Karsan argues the Federal Reserve, created to smooth the business cycle, has suppressed the periodic crises ('burning the underbrush') the system needs, so the eventual crisis becomes an immense forest fire.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Long-suppressed volatility implies a larger eventual crisis, favoring convex hedges.
insights.quote: Without a major crisis, without burning the underbrush, this will be an immense forest fire.

themes.theme: Dollar as weapon: Iran, Houthis, World War III

insights.claim: Karsan argues the US's greatest lever as the incumbent power is the US dollar, so under stress the strategy is to lean all over the dollar, while China tries to undermine it.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Dollar-dominance defense is the organizing principle behind US policy and geopolitics.
insights.quote: So once you are back on your heels and you see you are behind all of this stress and it's building and it's coming on you, you go to your greatest point of strength.

insights.claim: Karsan contends the US is in Iran for one reason: China had begun trading in yuan with Iran and making inroads in the Middle East and Venezuela, so the US is drawing a moat around the dollar by controlling Middle East trade, not because of nuclear weapons.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Middle East intervention should be modeled as currency-system defense, implying persistence despite costs.
insights.quote: It is quite frankly trying to draw a draw a moat around the US dollar by controlling trade on the Middle East.

insights.claim: Karsan says the US has made a little-publicized deal with the Houthis whereby trade through the Bab el-Mandeb strait is limited to American ships or those allowed to move, implying the majority of trade there is effectively US-controlled; he insinuates the US helped the Houthis gain control over the Saudis.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Shipping chokepoint control is being used as dollar-trade leverage, with costs to global trade.
insights.quote: the only trade that goes through there is American ships or those that are allowed to move.

insights.claim: Karsan states the world has entered World War III, an economic war with the US dollar at its center rather than a conventional one.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Expect war-footing economics: industrial policy, capital controls-like measures, and commodity stress.
insights.quote: This is an economic war with the US dollar at the center of it

insights.claim: Karsan argues US pressure on Europe is partly preemptive ally-building: Europe moving to a war footing, Ukraine being supported largely outside the US, and a more robust eastern front than five years ago, since a vassal-state Europe is a liability.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: European defense spending is a durable structural trend.
insights.quote: It is not helpful for the US to have a vassal state or in Europe.

insights.claim: The host counters that Europe may not be ready to stand alone, and if Europe cannot buy needed weapons from the US because the US is consuming them faster than it can produce, everyone becomes weaker.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Weapons production capacity is a binding constraint on Western rearmament.

themes.theme: Print money, buy stocks: US state capitalism

insights.claim: Karsan summarizes the administration's plan as 'print money, buy stocks': state industrial policy funded by taxing the world via dollar incumbency, monetizing the debt, and directly investing in strategic corporations as China has done for 20 years in solar, EVs, nuclear and rare earths.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Strategic-sector equities stand to benefit from direct state capital alongside debt monetization.
insights.quote: At at the end of the day, let's just summarize it as print money, buy stocks.

insights.claim: Karsan cites existing subtle steps toward this plan: Treasury buybacks supporting the long end of the curve, intervention in the yen so Japanese investors don't sell, and government stakes in companies such as Intel and MP Materials, none of which has happened to this extent outside a crisis.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Government equity stakes and curve support are precedents that will scale up in a crisis.
insights.quote: We have been supporting the long end of the curve through buybacks.

insights.claim: Karsan points to former Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson reappearing in April in a 45-minute Bloomberg interview warning of a coming Treasury crisis and calling for a facility to backstop the Treasury market, as a telegraph of what is coming.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: A formal Treasury-market backstop facility is a likely crisis-response tool.
insights.quote: There's a coming Treasury crisis

insights.claim: Karsan cites Japan as precedent: the BOJ owns about 8% of the Nikkei and Japan printed money for 35 years with little net yen weakness relative to money printed, aided by US support, while also buying domestic and global stocks.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Debt monetization with state equity buying can persist for decades when backed by a reserve-currency ally.
insights.quote: Japan owns 8% of the Nikkei.

insights.claim: Karsan says the US case is harder than Japan's: Japan was a cohesive export economy, whereas the US is an import economy that must rebuild its entire domestic production infrastructure while being challenged by China, requiring far more internal investment.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: US reshoring capex needs are enormous, supporting a hot, inflationary economy.
insights.quote: US is the import economy, right?

insights.claim: Karsan expects the plan to produce a hot economy with inflation in the US and even worse inflation abroad, as the US exports massive inflation while benefits accrue to US corporations and infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Position for global inflation with relative outperformance of US assets versus the rest of the world.
insights.quote: we export massive inflation. We also get inflation here in the US.

insights.claim: Karsan describes the catch-22: giving people money shifts from a supply-side to a demand-side model, which hurts margins and compresses multiples, so the plan is instead to give people stock (e.g., via a sovereign wealth fund) to short-circuit the K-shaped economy, a form of right-wing populism.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Policy may channel populist transfers through equity ownership, supporting valuations.
insights.quote: so what they're doing is essentially going to give people stock and say hey in 20 years you can spend this

insights.claim: Karsan links the stock-ownership plan to AI: if labor becomes less needed, a path toward something like universal basic income could resolve as 'everybody owns the AI' and receives its earnings.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: AI displacement could be addressed via broad equity ownership rather than taxation.
insights.quote: hey everybody owns the AI

insights.claim: Karsan cautions the plan faces resistance: China will be 'punching', there are internal incentives to burn it down, and corporations have incentives not to fall in line.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Execution risk on the dollar-centric plan is high, adding tail outcomes.
insights.quote: everybody's got a a plan till they get punched in the mouth

insights.claim: Karsan envisions a preferred endgame where the dollar stays dominant, the US regains footing, and after some resolution a new Bretton Woods renormalizes the system.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: A monetary-system reset is a plausible medium-term outcome to hedge for.
insights.quote: that there is a new kind of Bretton Woods that that renormalizes things.

insights.claim: Karsan argues QE-scale policy has never been deployed without a crisis, and the unanimity and buy-in needed for this level of policy necessitates a crisis.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: The massive policy response investors may expect requires a market crisis first.
insights.quote: we have not seen QE, I want to be clear, without a crisis, right?

insights.claim: Karsan predicts a meaningful crisis before June 2027 that will be allowed, to some extent, to happen so policymakers can deploy a massive response to otherwise unsustainable pressures, calling the midterms a massive inflection point.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Hedge for a policy-tolerated drawdown within roughly seven months, followed by aggressive intervention.
insights.quote: really before June of 27, you know, we believe there'll be a meaningful crisis that will be allowed essentially to happen to some extent

insights.claim: Karsan recalls saying five years ago that if the US did not act then, in ten years it would be too late, and says that despite disagreeing with Trump's handling, those around him understand incentives force aggressive action.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Expect continued aggressive, unconventional policy regardless of political setbacks.
insights.quote: if the US doesn't act now I said this 5 years ago, that in 10 years it will be too late.

insights.claim: Karsan says passive investing will not work well going forward and investors must be proactive; having called the break in bonds, he implies passive equities are what breaks next, though not on a one-week or one-month horizon.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Reduce reliance on passive beta; regime risk is skewed against buy-and-hold.
insights.quote: We said that before the bond part broke. Guess what breaks next?

insights.claim: Karsan argues the stability of a 60/40 portfolio, or its opposite, is merely a function of big cycles, so rather than betting on predictions investors should build resilience and only lean into macro bets at the margins.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Portfolio construction should be cycle-agnostic rather than dependent on a 40-year supply-side regime persisting.
insights.quote: are functions of big cycles, nothing more, nothing less.

insights.claim: Karsan's four portfolio building blocks: (1) active, fundamental ownership of what you understand (as Buffett and Howard Marks do), (2) diversification into uncorrelated assets, (3) holding insurance and monetizing it to redeploy ('gas and brakes'), and (4) using precise tools such as options for capital-efficient, diversified risk.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Combine hedges with a disciplined monetization process, using options for capital efficiency.
insights.quote: Three, the whole gas and brakes, you have insurance in your portfolio and monetize it.

insights.claim: Karsan claims these principles are undergraduate finance (U of Chicago Finance 101/201) yet 95-98% of the world ignores them.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Edge comes from applying basics most investors skip, not exotic insight.

insights.claim: The host argues retail access to leveraged products such as triple-leveraged short ETFs has handed investors risks they don't understand, and that such access is hard to roll back once given.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Retail leverage amplifies the potential severity of the coming crisis.
